# Signing and distribution {#sec-distribution}

A package is ready to ship when the user's operating system trusts it. On macOS and Windows,
that trust comes from a signature.

## Why sign {#sec-why-sign}

macOS and Windows check where downloaded software comes from. An unsigned app gets a stern
warning on Windows (SmartScreen) and is blocked outright on macOS (Gatekeeper) until the
user overrides it.

A signature proves two things: **who** published the app, and that **nobody changed it**
since. Unsigned builds are fine for development and a course project. Anything you hand to
users should be signed.

## macOS: Developer ID and notarization {#sec-sign-macos}

Apps distributed outside the Mac App Store need three things:

1. **A Developer ID certificate**, from the Apple Developer Program.
2. **A signature on every binary**, made with the *hardened runtime* and a secure timestamp.
3. **Notarization**: you upload the app to Apple, Apple scans it and issues a ticket, and you
   *staple* the ticket to the app so Gatekeeper accepts it even offline.

Qt's deploy tool signs the bundle for you when you pass it an identity. Use the
certificate's SHA-1 hash, which `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` lists: the deploy
script would split a name with spaces into several arguments.

```{.cmake filename="src/app/CMakeLists.txt"}
qt_generate_deploy_qml_app_script(TARGET app OUTPUT_SCRIPT deploy_script
    DEPLOY_TOOL_OPTIONS "-sign-for-notarization=${APP_SIGNING_IDENTITY}"
)
```

Then sign the disk image, notarize it and staple the ticket:

```sh
codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)" \
    --timestamp Sketchbook.dmg
xcrun notarytool submit Sketchbook.dmg --keychain-profile notary --wait
xcrun stapler staple Sketchbook.dmg
```

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Qt for macOS: deployment](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/macos-deployment.html),
[Apple: notarizing macOS software](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution)
:::

## Windows: Authenticode {#sec-sign-windows}

Windows signatures are called Authenticode. You sign the executable and the installer with
`signtool` from the Windows SDK:

```powershell
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /td SHA256 /a `
    /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com Sketchbook.exe
signtool verify /pa Sketchbook.exe
```

The certificate comes from a certificate authority or from a cloud signing service, such as
Microsoft's. Always add a timestamp (`/tr`): it keeps the signature valid after the
certificate expires. SmartScreen builds trust in a publisher over time, as more users install
its signed releases.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Microsoft: code signing options](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/code-signing-options),
[SignTool](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/signtool)
:::

## Signing in the pipeline {#sec-sign-pipeline}

The order matters:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    B[Build] --> T[Test] --> D[Deploy] --> S1[Sign app]
    S1 --> P[Package] --> S2[Sign package] --> N["Notarize<br/>(macOS)"]
```

- **Sign after deploying.** The deploy tool still changes binaries, and any change breaks a
  signature.
- **Sign inside out.** Libraries and plugins first, then the app, then the disk image or
  installer that contains it.
- **Treat certificates as secrets.** They live in your CI's secret store, never in the
  repository, and only release builds use them.

## App stores {#sec-stores}

App stores take over trust and updates, in exchange for their rules: a sandbox, a review, a
store package format.

| Store | Platform | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mac App Store | macOS | App Sandbox required |
| Microsoft Store | Windows | MSIX packages; `windeployqt --appx` prepares one (Qt 6.11+) |
| Google Play, App Store | Android, iOS | the normal way to ship mobile apps (@sec-mobile) |

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Microsoft Store deployment with windeployqt](https://www.qt.io/blog/windows-store-deployment-with-windeployqt)
:::
